idiom_name: DRb.start_service(uri, front_object) with a DRbObject client proxy; grpc gem
implementation_notes: dRuby ships the pattern in the standard library: DRb.start_service('druby://host:port', front_object) publishes one facade object, DRbObject.new_with_uri is the client-side proxy that forwards method calls and marshals arguments by copy, and the front object should expose only coarse use-case methods. The gRPC Ruby gem is the cross-language alternative with protobuf messages as payloads. The classic hand-written structure is the choice only when the peer cannot run Ruby and no schema is acceptable; otherwise DRb's transparency is hard to beat for a Ruby-to-Ruby boundary, provided its security model is understood.
code_sketch:
class OrderFacade                       # front object: coarse methods, no domain logic
  def place_order(customer, lines)
    order = Order.create(customer, lines)             # fine-grained objects
    to_confirmation(order, Pricing.price(order))      # payload
  end
end

DRb.start_service('druby://localhost:8787', OrderFacade.new)
DRb.thread.join
# client: facade = DRbObject.new_with_uri('druby://localhost:8787'); facade.place_order(c, lines)
pitfalls: DRb forwards method calls generically and reachable instance_eval lets a remote caller execute arbitrary Ruby on the server: publish a narrow front object, configure an ACL or TLS, and never expose the whole application object.
Marshalled arguments and results are copies, not shared references, so mutations made remotely are invisible locally and vice versa; return immutable value objects.

A remote reference does not keep the referenced object alive - dRuby does not prevent garbage collection, so long-lived remote objects must be retained by the server (or wrapped with the timer-based id converter).
